title: Chemical Reactions in Everyday Life

standard_text: Chemical reactions in everyday lives: evidence of chemical change; combustion, rusting, cooking, fermentation and neutralization; balanced equations; factors that change reaction rates in the kitchen and industry. meta_desc: Free Grade 11 General Science worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Term 2): signs of chemical change, types of reactions, balancing equations, combustion and rusting, and reaction rates. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: In a chemical reaction new substances form.
key_sub: Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.
body_html:
How to think about it

Chemical reactions happen all around us: wood and LPG burn (combustion), iron rusts, food cooks and spoils, dough rises by fermentation, and antacids neutralize stomach acid. Signs of a reaction include a color change, gas bubbles, heat or light, and a new solid.

A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. Reactions go faster at higher temperatures, with smaller pieces (more surface area), with higher concentrations and with catalysts, which is why we refrigerate food and chop vegetables to cook them faster.

Example

Balance: CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

Count O last

Answer: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

Example

Why does food spoil slower in a refrigerator?

Temperature

Answer: reactions are slower at low temperature

Common mistakes

  • Changing formulas to balance equations.
  • Thinking melting is a chemical change.
  • Thinking a catalyst is used up.

faq.a: Salt water speeds up the reaction of iron with oxygen and water.

items.e: Combustion: burning in oxygen. Thermal decomposition: heat breaks one compound into simpler ones. Neutralization: acid + alkali → salt + water.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
c: Yes. Both sides have the same elements.
No. There are too many arrows.
No. H has 8 atoms on the left and 6 on the right.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: Which change can be easily reversed?
items.e: Ice can melt back into water.

items.q: Is melting chocolate reversible?
c: Yes, it sets again when it cools.
No, it makes a new material.
items.e: Change of state.

items.q: What is an irreversible change?
c: a change that makes a new material and cannot easily be undone
items.e: Burning, cooking, rusting.

items.q: Lemonade powder is stirred into water and the water turns yellow. Is a new substance formed?
c: No. The powder dissolves and colors the water, making a mixture.
items.e: The powder only dissolves. The color comes from the powder spreading through the water.

items.q: Which is a physical change?
items.e: No new substance forms.

items.q: Composting food scraps is which kind of change?
items.e: Food scraps break down into compost.

items.q: Which is a physical change to a piece of paper?
c: letting it turn yellow in the sun for years
items.e: Folding changes the shape only. It is still paper.

items.q: Why is burning dangerous to investigate?
c: It gives out heat and flames that can cause burns and fires.
items.e: Only with adult supervision.

items.q: Can a cooked egg be uncooked?
c: No, cooking is an irreversible change.
items.e: The proteins have changed for good.

items.q: What happens to the yield of ammonia if ammonia is removed as it forms?
c: the equilibrium shifts right, so more ammonia forms
items.e: Removing a product makes the system replace it.

items.q: A campfire is fanned to supply more oxygen. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Higher oxygen concentration means more collisions.

items.q: Charcoal is burned as large lumps instead of small pieces. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Less surface area is exposed to oxygen.

items.q: Hydrogen peroxide is stored in a cool, dark place. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Lower temperature and no light slow its decomposition.

items.q: A catalyst is added to H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2HI (making hydrogen iodide) at equilibrium. What happens?
c: the position of equilibrium does not change; equilibrium is reached faster
the equilibrium shifts to the right
the equilibrium shifts to the left
items.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

items.q: Which change would NOT increase the rate of reaction between zinc and hydrochloric acid?
items.e: Larger lumps have less surface area.

items.q: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann diagram, how does a catalyst change the picture?
c: the activation energy line moves to the left, so more particles have enough energy
items.e: The distribution itself does not change.

items.q: Marble chips are crushed into powder. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: More surface area exposes more particles to collisions.

items.q: Why are enzymes important industrial catalysts?
c: they work only at high temperature
they work at low temperatures and are very specific, saving energy
items.e: Enzymes are used in detergents and food processing.

items.q: The acid is cooled in an ice bath. What happens to the reaction rate?
items.e: Slower particles collide less often and with less energy.

items.q: Enzymes in saliva are added to starch. Which explains the change in rate?
c: Slower particles collide less often and with less energy.
More particles in the same volume collide more often.
Fewer particles per volume means fewer collisions.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: The reaction mixture is stirred constantly. Which explains the change in rate?
c: Stirring brings fresh reactant particles together.
Higher pressure packs gas particles closer, so they collide more often.
Lower temperature slows the reactions that spoil food.
More particles in the same volume collide more often.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
c: it shifts the equilibrium to the right
it provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy
it gives the molecules more energy
items.e: More molecules then have at least the activation energy.

items.q: The acid is cooled in an ice bath. Which explains the change in rate?
c: Less surface area is exposed to oxygen.
Stirring brings fresh reactant particles together.
Particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have enough energy.
Slower particles collide less often and with less energy.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: On a graph of volume of gas against time, what does a steeper slope mean?
c: less gas is made in total
items.e: Rate = gradient of the curve.

items.q: A catalyst is added to CH<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ CO + 3H<sub>2</sub> (steam reforming) at equilibrium. What happens?
c: the equilibrium shifts to the left
the equilibrium shifts to the right
the position of equilibrium does not change; equilibrium is reached faster
items.e: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

items.q: The acid is diluted with water. Which explains the change in rate?
c: Lower temperature slows the reactions that spoil food.
Particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have enough energy.
Fewer particles per volume means fewer collisions.
items.e: Collision theory.

items.q: Charcoal is burned as large lumps instead of small pieces. Which explains the change in rate?

items.q: Why does increasing concentration increase the rate of reaction?
c: there are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent
items.e: Rate depends on collision frequency.

items.q: Why do most collisions not lead to a reaction?
c: the particles do not have enough energy or the right orientation
items.e: Successful collisions need E ≥ E<sub>a</sub>.
